source: Gobet (1997) A pattern-recognition theory of search in expert problem solving: claims
finding: Opened the full text (Gobet 1997, Thinking and Reasoning 3, 291-313; Brunel preprint). Templates (chunks grown into cores with slots) are said to help search in three ways: fast storage into long-term memory, a search in template space as well as move space (meta-search or abstract planning), and less loss in the mind's eye from decay and interference. The paper does NOT claim that templates simply cut the number of nodes.
numbers: Two opposite effects stated: pattern recognition makes deep search cheaper than weak methods, but it also removes the need for deep search because recognised evaluations are more reliable. These cancel, which is why depth differs only slightly by skill.
quote: the need for deep search often disappears because evaluations suggested by pattern recognition may be more reliable than evaluations computed by weak methods
limits: Theory paper plus simulation. The 'shorten search' wording is a reading of the abstract; the text says search can be both deeper and less needed.
agent_relevance: S0: a recognition pass is not a promise of a shorter trace. It may enable deeper checks of the move it suggests. Test token cost, not only accuracy.

source: Gobet (1997) SEARCH model: simulated depth, speed and stopping by net size
finding: SEARCH program (1,000 episodes per net size) predicts mean depth and rate of search rise as a power function of the number of chunks. Chunks and templates replace slow heuristic move generation. Stop reasons shift toward 'evaluation by recognition'.
numbers: Mean depth: under 1 ply with no chunks; about 2.5 ply at 1,000 chunks; about 4 ply at 30,000 chunks (expert); over 5 ply above 100,000 chunks (grandmaster). Regression from Charness (1981): 2.3 ply at 1300 Elo, 4.1 at 2000, 5.7 at grandmaster. Time per heuristic move 20 s, per heuristic evaluation 10 s, per mental move 2 s, pattern-based move generation about 0 (few hundred ms). Episodes ended by evaluation: about 75% with large nets (at the start about 65% ended because no move was proposed and a little under 25% because of fuzziness). Template probability is about log of chunks (r2 = .94); templates about linear in chunks (r2 = .97), fitted with CHREST on 50 master-game positions.
limits: Parameters are set by the author, partly from CHREST and CHUMP runs; the model is fitted, not independently tested. Model rate of search is higher than human data (Gobet in press: 4.8, 4.1, 3.2, 3.4 nodes per minute for Master, Expert, Class A, Class B).
agent_relevance: Recognition replaces slow move generation first (time cost), and stopping by recognised evaluation is the main saving. A schema could log the stop reason (recognised vs computed).

source: Gobet (1997) test against Saariluoma (1990): non-monotone depth
finding: SEARCH is checked against the one anomaly in the human data: Saariluoma found top players search less than masters. The model reproduces dips only when trial numbers are small (50 episodes), so the author calls the anomaly sampling noise.
numbers: Saariluoma 1990: masters (about 2200 Elo) searched 52 nodes at 5.1 average depth; IMs and grandmasters 23 nodes at 3.6. Simulation with 50 episodes per net size (about 5 players x 10 episodes) shows a power-curve increase with dips and peaks.
limits: Explains away rather than predicts; Campitelli and Gobet (2004, d04) later found a strong linear skill effect in depth with harder positions, which fits the power law but not the 'search is flat' story.
agent_relevance: Do not use 'experts search the same as novices' as a design rule; it holds only for easy positions.

source: Campitelli & Gobet (2004) Adaptive expert decision making: skilled chessplayers search more and deeper (ICGA Journal 27, 209-216)
finding: With very hard positions (solutions needing 52, 60 and 70+ nodes and up to 23-35 ply), search volume, depth and speed rose strongly and linearly with rating. Earlier 'flat search' findings came from easy positions and verbal protocols.
numbers: N = 4 (GM 2550, IM 2500, CM 2100, class B 1750), 3 positions, think-aloud. Nodes generated: GM 370, IM 405, CM 153, CB 88. Mean depth (ply): 13.8, 10.5, 7.4, 2.8. Max depth: 25, 23.7, 17.7, 10.5. Rate: 12.3, 13.5, 6.8, 3.2 nodes/min. Regressions: mean depth = -18.3 + 0.012 Elo (r = .97); nodes = -645 + 0.4 Elo (r = .96). Top players in older studies: 35, 58, 23 nodes (average 38.6) vs 387.5 here, ten times more; older mean depth 5.4, 3.6, 5 ply vs 13.8 and 10.5.
limits: Four players, one per level, only 2 above master; r with N = 4 is fragile. Think-aloud may distort.
agent_relevance: Search quality scales with skill when the task needs it. Our scaffold should let search depth grow with problem difficulty, not cap it at a few candidates.

source: Campitelli & Gobet (2004) second block: fast decisions and recall
finding: Same 4 players, 10-second decisions on easy tactical positions (5 s display plus 5 s black screen) and a recall test. Under time pressure skill separated players by accuracy, which the authors attribute to stored knowledge letting experts evaluate fast. A simple reaction-time task showed no skill difference.
numbers: Livshitz positions needing 10.4 nodes (sd 4.2), depth 6.4 ply: correct GM 23 (46.9%), IM 18 (36.9%), CM 4 (8.2%), CB 2 (4.1%); r(4) = .94 with Elo. Recall of game positions 83.2%, 85%, 54%, 47% (GM, IM, CM, CB).
limits: N = 4; one source paper for both claims.
agent_relevance: The same players do both: quick recognition under pressure, wide search when allowed. Supports an S0 gate with an escalation path, not a fixed mode.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) Mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements (PLoS ONE 8, e75796)
finding: Replicated the eye-movement result of Bilalic et al. 2008 in a choose-a-move task: players who chose the familiar, suboptimal move kept looking at its region, and experts who found the better move gradually looked away. Experts and novices were equally prone to the suboptimal Einstellung move. New boundary condition: when the familiar move was a blunder, the effect vanished.
numbers: N = 34 (17 experts, mean CFC rating 2223, range 1876-2580; 17 novices). Problem 1 (Einstellung move good but suboptimal): 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose it. Problems 2-4 (Einstellung move a blunder): all experts and most novices avoided it. Experts looked at the target region sooner (407 ms vs 719 ms, p < .01) with shorter dwells (2395 vs 3440 ms, p < .05) and more dwells (27 vs 18); total dwell time equal (52.0 s vs 51.4 s).
limits: Small N, four problems, one lab. The authors suggest the blunder case worked because it gave feedback that the familiar solution failed.
agent_relevance: A fast first answer that is good enough blocks the better one, even for experts; a first pass that visibly fails does not. Gate S0 so a plausible-but-weak match triggers a forced search for alternatives.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung effect (Cognition)
finding: Candidate masters who found the familiar five-move smothered mate said they were hunting for a shorter mate, but eye tracking showed they kept looking at squares of the familiar solution. Those who saw only the short-solution problem looked increasingly at the new squares and found it. Players who had met the familiar solution first were slower even on a later problem that no longer contained it.
numbers: Exp 1: group with the familiar solution all stopped at the smothered mate after about 37 s (SD 20); later found the 3-move mate in a mean 148 s (SD 90) vs 79 s (SD 25) for players who saw only the 1-solution problem. Gaze share on solution squares: time x squares interaction F(5,20) = 11.9, p < .001 (no-Einstellung group), F(5,20) = 0.6 ns (Einstellung group). Exp 2: players without prior exposure solved in about half the time, t(44) = 2.16, p = .036, d = .65. Effect size from the series: IM (5 SD above mean) with a familiar solution performed like Class A (2 SD); Masters like Class B; Candidate Masters like Class C, about 3 SDs (about 600 Elo) lost.
quote: the presence of a familiar solution that first came to mind reduced the problem solving performance of the experts to that of players about three standard deviations lower
limits: Preprint of the published paper; the 3-SD figure is quoted from the paper's summary of earlier work (Bilalic et al. 2008, Cognitive Psychology), not re-derived here. Small groups per skill level.
agent_relevance: Measured cost of a plausible first answer on experts: about 3 SD of skill. An LLM first pass should force one alternative-search step with a different cue (the failure is attention, not missing knowledge).

source: Robbins et al. (1996) Working memory in chess (Memory & Cognition 24, 83-93)
finding: Primary data for the Charness vs Bradley dispute. Blocking the visuospatial sketchpad or the central executive cut recall of 10-s-viewed master positions and the quality of tactical moves; blocking the articulatory loop did nothing. No difference between weak and strong players in any experiment.
numbers: Exp 1 (N = 20; weaker n = 12, stronger n = 8): recall score (stronger) control 40.4, articulatory 37.1, visuospatial 16.3, executive 20.9 (a fall of 60% and 48%); weaker 2.9, 3.3, -4.8, -9.8 (near floor, corrected score). F(3,54) = 6.83, p < .01; skill x condition F(3,54) = 1.08 ns. Exp 2 tactical problems (about 12 players): stronger control 30.3, AL 27.8, VSSP 19.0, CE 19.0 (-37%); weaker 16.7, 17.3, 10.3, 10.7 (-38% and -36%). F(3,30) = 3.47, p < .05. Correlation with rating r = .78 (recall), r = .70 (tactics).
limits: Power for the skill x condition test was about 20% for a medium effect (authors). The 'over two thirds' recall drop is NOT reproduced here (about half for strong players); that number is second-hand (Gobet and Simon 1996) and may come from the unpublished Bradley thesis.
agent_relevance: Recognition and search both need visuospatial or executive resources, so the 'two separate systems' split is weak. Do not build an S0 that assumes recognition is free of load.

source: Dispute check: Charness (1976) vs Bradley/Robbins (1996) as different paradigms
finding: Cross-check from the opened Robbins paper and Gobet and Simon's review (a14): Charness (1976) used a 30-s interfering delay AFTER presentation; Robbins/Bradley used a secondary task DURING a 10-s study period. So the 6-8% and 'over two thirds' numbers come from different manipulations and do not directly contradict each other.
numbers: Charness 1976: 30 s delay cut recall 6-8%. Robbins 1996: concurrent visuospatial or executive load cut strong-player recall by 48-60% and tactics by about 37%.
limits: Charness 1976 itself not opened (only the Crossref record, DOI 10.1037/0278-7393.2.6.641, confirmed). The dispute is resolved as 'different task timing', not as a failed replication.
agent_relevance: Load while encoding hurts; delay after encoding does not. For an LLM, distraction in context during first read may matter more than later noise.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Appendix B: policy-only Leela bot rated over 2600 on Lichess
finding: Found the primary statement in Jenner et al. Appendix B (opened PDF). A Lichess bot using only Leela's policy network is said to have blitz and rapid ratings over 2600, with an archived link to the bot's page. The authors note this is below the best humans, and their own network is slightly larger and likely stronger.
numbers: Claim: Lichess ratings above 2600 (blitz and rapid) for a policy-only Leela bot (account LazyBot, archive dated May 2024). Authors' network: slightly larger, likely stronger.
limits: Reported by link to an archived page, not a controlled study. I did not open the archived page (third-party archive). Lichess ratings are not FIDE Elo and bots meet bot-heavy pools.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 closed as documented-but-secondary: cite as 'reported by Jenner et al. via a Lichess page', not as a measurement.

source: McIlroy-Young et al. (2020) Aligning superhuman AI with human behavior: Stockfish matching range and tree-search effect
finding: Located the missing figure. Stockfish at depths 1-15 matches human moves 33-41% of the time; the best Stockfish and Leela models reach 46%; Maia (policy network, no tree search) reaches over 52%. Adding 10 MCTS rollouts to Maia hurts, as does removing move history.
numbers: Stockfish depth 1-15: 33-41% move matching; depth 15 matches 1900-rated players 5 points more than 1100-rated. Leela max 46%. Maia lowest accuracy (trained on 1900, tested on 1100) 46%; Maia highest over 52%. History of the last 12 plies: +3 points; no tree search: +5 to +10 points; more rollouts: no gain.
quote: tree search ... tends to degrade move prediction performance in our setting
limits: Move-matching is agreement with human moves in 1100-1900 Lichess games, not win rate. Maia plays weaker than Stockfish.
agent_relevance: A quick-pass module should imitate people when the task is predicting or explaining human choices; use engine-style supervision when only correctness matters. Search on top of a human-imitating policy made agreement worse.

source: Kolasani et al. (2025) LLM Chess: reasoning effort and cost scaling
finding: Over 50 LLMs vs a random opponent; reasoning models far ahead of non-reasoning models; more reasoning tokens help; 3-way and 5-way mixture-of-agents (parallel samples) gave no clear extra gain. Best Elo estimate is low.
numbers: Win rate vs random: reasoning models 45.4% average, non-reasoning 0.7%; instruction-following errors 24.4% vs 71.9%. Best model (o3, low effort) about 758 Elo (engine skill levels 250-1375 Elo); chess.com user average 611. Scaling reasoning effort: up to +15% (low to medium) and +20% (low to high) win rate. 3x MoA of o4-mini (low) with o4-mini (medium) aggregator slightly above o4-mini (medium); 5x slightly lower. At least 30 games per Elo estimate.
limits: No equal-token-budget comparison across models; effort levels are the vendor setting, and high effort timed out more often. Elo is against one engine family.
agent_relevance: Spending tokens deeper (sequential) helped; spending them wider (parallel) did not, in chess. Prefer deeper checks of few lines over wide sampling.

source: Liu et al. (2026) ChessArena: Glicko ratings, Bullet mode, puzzles
finding: 13 LLMs, over 800 games, four modes. No LLM beat Maia-1100. Banning visible thinking (Bullet mode) made nearly all models play badly. Only the o3 model scored above 15% on multi-step puzzles.
numbers: Glicko: Maia-1100 2220 (44 games), o3 1830, Doubao-Seed-1-6-Thinking 1776, Gemini-2.5-Pro 1699, fine-tuned Qwen3-8B-Chess 1686 (Blitz, 182 games), GPT-4.1 1583. Puzzles: Stockfish 98.4%, Maia-1100 74.6%, o3 55.6%, all other LLMs under 15%. Token caps: 4,096 for non-thinking, 16,384 for thinking models.
limits: Not an equal token budget (4k vs 16k). Ratings are on the platform's own Glicko scale with about 30 games per model and wide intervals (RD 50-93).
agent_relevance: A quick pass without reasoning loses badly on tactics; one-shot recognition by the LLM is not enough. Keep an S0 escape to explicit search.

source: Hwang et al. (2025) Can LLMs develop strategic reasoning? Post-training insights from learning chess
finding: RL with a dense reward from a chess action-value network beat sparse rewards but every model plateaued at 25-30% puzzle accuracy. Adding 1,000 o3 reasoning traces by SFT did not move the ceiling, and Llama3.1-8B fell. The authors blame missing chess knowledge from pretraining.
numbers: Plateau 25-30% Lichess puzzle accuracy; reference 1800-Elo searchless transformer 66.5% (Ruoss). Chess knowledge probes: board-state accuracy 0.0% for all six base and instruct models; MATE accuracy 12.7% to 53.7% (Qwen2.5-3B-It 53.7%).
limits: Small models (3B-8B) only; puzzle accuracy not matched to token use.
agent_relevance: Reasoning on top of weak recognition does not help: the quick pass must carry domain knowledge first. A scaffold cannot make up for a missing pattern store.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally: search vs best-of-N by difficulty
finding: On MATH, beam search with a process verifier beats best-of-N only on harder questions. On easy questions beam search got worse as the budget rose (exploiting verifier errors). Choosing the method by estimated difficulty cut compute about 4x at equal accuracy. A smaller model plus test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model on easy and medium questions, but not on the hardest.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with up to about 4x less test-time compute; FLOPs-matched comparison against a 14x larger model. Beam search (beam width 4): worse than best-of-N on difficulty levels 1-2, better on levels 3-4, no real progress at level 5.
limits: PaLM 2-S* on MATH only; difficulty bins come from the base model's own success rate. Compares search with sampling, not with a recognition-first pass.
agent_relevance: Direct measured support for a difficulty gate: search helps where the policy is weak, hurts where it is already right. Closest LLM test of the S0 idea.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: search over policy-only chain-of-thought (Game of 24)
finding: GPT-4 chain-of-thought solved 4% of Game of 24 problems; breadth-5 tree search with LLM-scored partial thoughts solved 74%. Even breadth 1 gave 45%. ToT used about as many tokens as 100 CoT samples and was more accurate than best-of-100.
numbers: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k = 100) 9.0%, ToT b = 1 45%, ToT b = 5 74%, CoT best of 100 49%, IO best of 100 33%. Cost per case: ToT 5.5k completion + 1.4k prompt tokens, $0.74, 74%; CoT best of 100 6.7k + 2.2k tokens, $0.47, 49%; IO best of 100 1.8k + 1.0k tokens, $0.13, 33%.
limits: One task type (arithmetic search with three steps). The CoT 4% is low compared with other reports of GPT-4 on this task, so the gain depends on the baseline prompt. Math and code beyond Game of 24 not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Measured gain of search over a policy-only pass: about 70 points on a search-heavy task at about the tokens of 100 samples.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: retrieved reusable thought templates
finding: A library (meta-buffer) of high-level thought templates is retrieved by a problem-distiller and instantiated for the problem at hand. Gains over the same base model with CoT, and cost about 12% of tree/graph-of-thought style multi-query methods.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-4 3.0%, GPT-4 + CoT 11.0%, PAL 64.0%, ToT 74.0%, GoT 73.2%, Meta-prompting 67.0%, BoT 82.4%. Reported gains over previous best: +11% Game of 24, +20% Geometric Shapes, +51% Checkmate-in-One. Cost about 12% of multi-query methods on average. Size study: Llama3-8B + BoT 78.4 vs Llama3-70B 73.4 on Game of 24 (read from the figure).
limits: Authors' own runs; templates are code-like programs, so this is closer to a stored solver than to a human template. Measured transfer is to new instances of the same task family; no cross-task transfer test and no isolation of slot-filling (ablations remove the distiller and the meta-buffer only).
agent_relevance: Gap 6 only partly closed: slot-filled template retrieval is measurable and cheap in tokens. Suggests a template store with named slots, tested on held-out instances of the same family.

source: Wang et al. (2023) SwiftSage: fast module with slow module called only when needed
finding: A small fast policy acts by default; an LLM planner is invoked only on hard states. Tokens per action fell by more than half versus ReAct-style agents while scoring higher on ScienceWorld.
numbers: Tokens per action: SayCan 1,855.84, ReAct 1,971.03, Reflexion 2,983.46, SwiftSage 757.07 (about 62% fewer than ReAct, 75% fewer than Reflexion).
limits: The fast module is a trained behaviour-cloned T5 model, not an LLM; benchmark is ScienceWorld text-games. Agents differ in many ways beyond fast/slow.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 closed in direction: a recognition-first pass with gated escalation cut tokens and kept or raised score in an agent task. Not yet shown for single-answer reasoning.
